drafts.title: 20,860 gallons of gas: Aspen's chargers are so busy it just added 14 more plugs
drafts.angle: Chargers on the Western Slope are busy, not empty. Aspen just added 14 public plugs because the old ones run 60% busy in peak season. Make it local: Garfield County is part of the 4,400 EV count, and that's the I-70 stretch you drive.
bullets: Aspen added 7 dual-port Level 2 stations, 14 new public spaces (ARC, Golf/Nordic, Truscott, Red Brick). Network went from 12 plugs in 2021 to 38.
More than 4,400 registered EVs across Pitkin, Eagle and Garfield counties, about 6% of vehicles in Aspen Electric territory.
Several sites top 60% use in peak season; 20% is considered a strong benchmark. South Spring St: 69% of peak visits found it already in use.
2025 network delivered 231,310 kWh, about 20,860 gallons of gas displaced.
drafts.body: 20,860 gallons of gas. That's what Aspen's public chargers replaced last year. Now they added 14 more plugs because the old ones sit 60% busy in peak season. Over in Grand Junction I usually charge {where I charge most}. Ever pulled up to a full charger on the Western Slope?
drafts.framework_body:
20,860 gallons of gas.

That's how much Aspen's public chargers replaced last year. And they're so busy the city just added 14 more plugs.

Here's the number that got me. A charger that's busy 20% of the time is considered a good one. Several of Aspen's run over 60% in peak season. At one spot on South Spring Street, 69% of the time somebody showed up, it was already taken.

There are now more than 4,400 EVs registered in Pitkin, Eagle and Garfield counties. Garfield is Glenwood, Rifle, Parachute. That's the I-70 stretch I drive. {my last trip up valley and where I charged}.

People keep telling me nobody wants these cars. Then why are the chargers full?

Busy chargers are a good problem. It means people bought the cars. The next step is more fast chargers between Glenwood and Grand Junction. {my one-line take on where the next one should go}.

{photo of the charger I use most}

Ever pulled up to a full charger on the Western Slope? Where?
drafts.ocr_why: Hard number opener, local Western Slope, first-hand fill-in and a question close. Builds on your I-70 gap and Palisade posts without repeating them.
drafts.pixel: Stand at {a GJ or valley charger}: "Aspen says its chargers are 60% busy. Here's what it looks like where I charge."
drafts.premium_target: Quote or reply to a verified Colorado EV or Tesla owner account posting about I-70 or mountain charging, keeping it to the busy-charger point; self-thread link back to your 42.7-mile gap post if it fits.

drafts.title: $99 a month to stay in your lane: what new Tesla buyers don't get anymore
drafts.angle: Owner-cost honesty. New Model 3 and Model Y buyers in the US and Canada no longer get basic Autosteer standard; it now comes with the $99/month FSD subscription. Two things can be true: FSD is great, and a $50k car should come with lane-keeping.
bullets: Since January 2026, new US and Canada Model 3 and Model Y ship with Traffic-Aware Cruise Control only; Autosteer moved behind FSD (Reuters, Jan 23).
FSD (Supervised) subscription is $99 a month.
Tesla reported 1.74 million active FSD users in Q3 2026; about 75% of new North America deliveries included FSD (Electrek).
Not a Tesla App reports Musk directed the cut to boost subscriptions; it's trending today.
drafts.body: $99 a month. That's what a new Model Y buyer now pays just to get the car to steer itself in its lane. Basic Autosteer isn't standard anymore. I {what I pay for FSD, or bought it outright} and use it {how often}. Worth it, or should lane-keeping come free?
drafts.framework_body:
$99 a month.

That's what a new Model 3 or Model Y buyer now pays to get the car to steer itself in its lane. Basic Autosteer used to come with the car. Since January, new cars in the US and Canada ship with plain cruise control instead. Lane-keeping now lives inside the FSD subscription.

Honest take from an owner. FSD is the best thing about my car. {one real moment where FSD helped me, not the Grand Mesa drive}. I {what I pay for FSD, or that I bought it outright}.

But my {older car or a friend's cheap car} keeps itself in the lane for free. A $50,000 car should too.

Tesla says 1.74 million people now pay for FSD. That tells me people like it. It doesn't tell me they should have to pay monthly for something that used to be standard.

Two things can be true. FSD is worth it to me. And basic lane-keeping should come free.

If you're shopping for a Tesla right now, would this change your mind? Or is $99 a month fair?
drafts.ocr_why: Dollar opener, owner first-hand, and a real debate that pulls replies from Tesla fans and skeptics alike.
drafts.pixel: In the driver's seat: "Here's what $99 a month gets you, and what new buyers don't get anymore."
drafts.premium_target: Quote a verified Tesla owner or creator account discussing the Autopilot cut (Sawyer Merritt if he covers it) with one opinion line: great product, but lane-keeping should be standard.

Heating is only about $542 of that $1,196; the rest is lights, appliances and water heating.

drafts.title: $3 billion lost by seniors, so now AI is answering the scam calls
drafts.angle: AI isn't only the scammer's tool. New AI bots pretend to be the confused victim, keep the crook talking, and pass what they learn to banks. AI for the masses: on our side for once. Keep the plain family defense in the close.
bullets: FTC data: losses reported by people over 60 rose from about $600M in 2020 to about $3B in 2025 (via Vox).
Apate.ai runs AI agents that pose as scam victims by phone, text and email, keep scammers talking, and pass what they learn to banks; CommBank in Australia uses it (TechCrunch, Oct 14).
Apate raised US$8.15M and reincorporated in the US.
The simple family defense still wins: hang up and call back on a number you already have.
drafts.body: $3 billion. That's what Americans over 60 reported losing to scams last year, up from $600 million in 2020. Now there's AI that answers scam calls, plays the confused victim, and wastes the crook's whole afternoon. {my reaction}. Would you let an AI pick up your spam calls?
drafts.framework_body:
$3 billion.

That's what Americans over 60 reported losing to scams last year. In 2020 it was about $600 million. Five times worse in five years.

Most of what you hear is AI making it worse. Fake voices. Fake grants. Fake grandkids in trouble.

So here's one I actually like. A company called Apate built AI that answers scam calls and plays the victim. It sounds confused. It asks the scammer to repeat things. It keeps them on the line for as long as it can. Meanwhile it's collecting the bank accounts and scripts they use, and handing it to banks so they can shut them down.

Every minute a crook spends talking to a robot is a minute he isn't talking to {a neutral family member, like someone's mom}.

{my reaction in one line}

The old rule still beats any app though. If someone calls about money, hang up and call back on a number you already have. Not the one they gave you.

Would you let an AI pick up your spam calls?
drafts.ocr_why: Big dollar opener, AI for the masses with a fun twist, and save-and-share appeal for adult kids and 55+ readers. Different from the code-word and VA grant posts.
drafts.pixel: To camera: "AI is fighting back against scammers. Here's the one thing I'd still tell {a neutral family member} anyway."
drafts.premium_target: Quote a verified AI or consumer-tech account sharing the Apate story (or an AARP or fraud-watch account) with the line: finally, AI on our side.

drafts.title: $300,000 a truck: a family trucking company just ordered 50 Tesla Semis
drafts.angle: A family-owned trucking company, not a tech giant, is betting on electric rigs. They tested one for 4,000 miles first and it matched the promise. Close on the I-70 winter question your audience knows.
bullets: Tesla Semi account: Chicago's first 50 Semis en route for delivery (Nov 11).
Buyer: HMD Trucking, family-owned, founded 1998, 650+ trucks, almost all diesel today.
Summer test: 4,000+ miles at 1.74 kWh per mile vs Tesla's 1.7 claim.
Deal about $15M, roughly $300,000 per truck; HMD is building its own depot chargers because Megachargers are mostly on I-5 and I-10.
drafts.body: $300,000 a truck, and a family trucking company in Chicago just ordered 50. They ran one 4,000 miles first. It used about what Tesla promised. With diesel at {what diesel costs in GJ today}, I get why. Would you trust an electric semi on I-70 in winter?
drafts.framework_body:
$300,000 a truck. And they ordered 50.

The buyer isn't Amazon or Pepsi. It's HMD Trucking, a family-owned outfit in Chicago that started in 1998 and runs about 650 trucks. Almost all diesel.

What I respect: they didn't just take Tesla's word for it. They ran one Semi more than 4,000 miles this summer. Tesla promised 1.7 kWh per mile. It did 1.74. Close enough to bet the business on.

They're also building their own chargers at the yard, because Tesla's big truck chargers are mostly out on I-5 and I-10. That's the honest part nobody likes to say. The trucks are ready before the chargers are.

Diesel in Grand Junction is {what diesel costs in GJ today}. {my one line on what that means for a trucker's fuel bill or for prices at the store}.

Would you trust an electric semi on I-70 over Vail Pass in January?
